article_text:
Three generations of women confront grief in The First Taste of Loneliness , the third entry in a trilogy from director Gu You. His debut film, Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains (2019), screened at Cannes. Dwelling by the West Lake followed in 2023.

First Taste stars the noted Chinese actor Zhou Xun as Jiang Yue, a divorced mother who recently lost a design job. She returns home to help her mother Luna (Xi Meijuan) care for her ailing husband. Yue’s daughter Moon (Wang Shengdi), a high school student, has trouble adapting to a life centered on her grandfather’s illness.

Working with Japanese cinematographer Mikiya Takimoto, Gu takes an arresting visual approach based in part on Chinese landscape paintings. Traveling from right to left, as if unscrolling a painting, the camera moves patiently through majestic landscapes and intimate interiors in shots that can extend several minutes.

The film’s sense of time is fluid, with past, present, and future mixing together within a single frame. On his iPhone, Gu pointed out how scroll paintings can combine together different times and settings. What’s pervasive in Gu’s film is a sense of loss, of life irrevocably changed by the presence of death.

We spoke with the director at the 2026 Busan International Film Festival, where the film premiered in the main competition and picked up two awards: Zhou Xun for Best Actor and Li Danfeng for Busan Award for Artistic Contribution Recipient, specifically for sound design.

The Film Stage: This is such a complex film. It must have been very difficult to make. Especially the cinematography. The camera is always moving. At times, to me, it seemed to be searching for water, for the river that provides a central visual motif.

Gu You: The camera is actually looking for family members. Those shots you mention find the three generations of women in and around water and the river. The camera is taking the grandfather’s point of view. When it sees Jiang Yue crying, it also looks for the rest of the family. You can say that this film is the last 100 days leading up to the grandfather’s passing. The camera is, in a sense, like his soul.

Can you talk about your visual approach? Why do you use extended takes?

The visuals are based on emotions and philosophy. But I would like to talk about techniques first. All three of my films are based on the Shanshui paintings, an ancient Chinese art form. We set up rules for shooting, the first being that the camera would always move from right to left. That refers to the way the old scrolls would be opened.

The second rule was to incorporate different settings and locations in one shot—a way to recreate the technique used in the scrolls, where you can see the flow or transition of space and time.

What I was trying to do was restrict how we shot in order to find new ways of making films. Because right now we see people using AI to create films. Anyone has access to every method of filmmaking. There’s no longer an “incorrect” style. I used my rules or principles to restrict or return to a more honest way of shooting—not only for Chinese films, but for films of all cultures.

Gu You

You have a shot at a mountain shrine that contains several timelines at once.

I intended it to imitate the point of view of the Shanshui paintings. Those paintings are very different from European paintings or photos. A picture in Europe might portray a character or a single point in time. Shanshui paintings contain many times and locations. You can think of cuts or edits as you unscroll. At one spot, you might see all four seasons.

We have what’s called a bird’s-eye view that flies over time and space in a Shanshui painting. It’s like traveling in a hot air balloon. For older Chinese, looking at a Shanshui painting is like watching a film in the past. They actually unroll the painting, so they are traveling along with it. The painting we use in the poster of the mountain and river, those trees in the foreground are actually from the summit. The painter just moved down to the front of the painting.

That’s an inspiration for my movie, because there is a time and space we can film, but it’s up to the viewer to combine them. For example, in the second long take, the montage is moving forward, but the story itself is going backwards.

There’s another take that viewers might find challenging. Jiang Yue and her mother Luna go to a restaurant to meet Mr. Xu and his family. At the beginning of the take, we see Xu washing his hands in the bathroom, but on the soundtrack we hear Xu introducing his family inside the restaurant. As the shot continues, we hear Xu at his table saying he is going to the men’s room. We could have edited it in a linear fashion, but I wanted to try to combine the entire scene in one space, regardless of time.

I’m curious how you design shots. There is a long track through Luna’s apartment that dwells on several details: photos, sculptures, plaques. Do you write or storyboard that shot, or is it more of a collaboration with the cinematographer?

The details of the more difficult shots we’ll draw or storyboard to explain what we want to the DP. But there is also a longer process. We rented that apartment for months before we started shooting. That way we could prep and rehearse for as long as we want. Let’s put it that most of the shots were designed by me and then executed by the DP.

But take the scene in the park at night, where Luna is dancing with Xu. When Xu leaves the shot, she continues dancing by herself. The camera circles around her, moving in to a close-up just as the waltz brings tears to her eyes. There are lights to deal with and a lot of extras behind her. The camera still has to find a way to capture Luna’s emotions.

You said earlier that this was a difficult film to make, and you’re right. Not just the long, long takes, but I’m working with actors who are very famous in China. We’re putting them out in public spaces where bystanders get very excited to see them.

What we had to do was rehearse when no one was there, like the middle of the night. We go over the routes they will take, how they will walk, how we will film them. When you get to the shoot, you get one take, one chance.

With that shot of Luna, we had hidden cameras to capture different angles, and we cast the actors behind her so we could match the shots. But if we fail to get what we want on the first take, we have to move to another location because all the onlookers will see we’re shooting a film.

That moment transcended the narrative. It became pure emotion. It’s remarkable you could get it, have the actress and DP work together so perfectly. There’s another shot at night: Moon and her boyfriend are running on an outdoor track with what look like hundreds of students in uniform.

We’re depicting high school life, and one special moment for students in China is the need to run very late at night. They can’t go to bed. They can’t sleep. They have to exercise. It’s a unique memory for high schoolers in China. The shot’s a concentrated version of the youth of these two characters. It was a bold choice because Moon’s boyfriend is very famous. He’s actually an idol in China.

Can you talk about the Teresa Teng song you use at the end?

I was young when heard “The First Taste of Loneliness.” The lyrics go, “The wind came over and asked me: What is loneliness? You are still young. What do you know about loneliness?” At the time, I didn’t understand the lyrics because I was so young. Now I’m older, I’ve experienced loss in my life, and I have a deeper understanding of the meaning of loneliness. That’s actually the main theme of the movie. I had this ending in mind from the start. I had it set before we started shooting. Later I constructed the story leading to it.

The movie shows three people, each of whom is saying goodbye to the past, then opening new chapters after the loss of the grandfather. I would say there are three parts to the movie. The first is the emotions of parting, then the experience of loneliness. The third plot line is a little hidden. Jiang Yue finds her father’s wish list. On it he had a goal of doing one kind act a day.

Jiang Yue at first thinks that means helping other people, like the elderly, or maybe donating money. That kindness is external. What’s more important is internal kindness. That is, express more love to your family and to those who are still living.

Are you comfortable leaving viewers with such a dark ending?

The ending is not so bright, I agree with you. But we hope that at least five people can have a taste of loneliness at the ending. The five being the three women, the passed grandpa, and most importantly, the audience.

Loneliness is almost like a background color in our life. It’s one of the basics. If we can think of the meaning of loneliness beforehand, before we have a taste of it, maybe we will be prepared. Perhaps we can face topics like life and death in films more seriously, maybe even optimistically. We can also have a better understanding of the meaning of life.

Life is good, but happiness is rare.

That’s the Buddhist thinking. We always say hardship is enlightenment. Struggle is enlightenment. I do believe in the existence of soul and spirit. If we experience a lot of hardship in this world, maybe we can store it in our souls. After we die, it can be turned into a spirit. I believe that is the core meaning of life.

The First Taste of Loneliness premiered at the 2026 Busan International Film Festival.

article_text:
Published by Loose Joints, Don’t Worry Boys borrows its title from a legendary New York gay club and revives the unbuttoned pleasures of the Hudson River piers, before AIDS turns the party into a wake.

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Stanley Stellar .

The book opens on a facsimile of a vermilion membership card: the Don’t Worry Boys Social Club “invites you to go to The Zoo,” at 421 West 13th Street. Stanley Stellar dates it, tentatively, to the late 1960s or early 1970s.

In 1976, the Brooklyn native took up photography and almost at once turned his lens on the gay community of the West Village, whose nights he shared.

His pictures ran in gay skin mags, in the newspaper New York Native and in Christopher Street , a literary magazine named after the Stonewall Inn’s street, where the founding riots of gay liberation erupted in 1969 after a police raid. A regular contributor to the magazine, the novelist Andrew Holleran, author of Dancer from the Dance (1978), discovered the photographs in its pages and saw in them “the street’s answer to Robert Mapplethorpe.”

In a New York magnetized by cruising, the street could turn the most ordinary run to the supermarket into a chance encounter. There, clothes advertised a man’s sexual role and appetites. Keys or a bandana worn on the left marked a top; on the right, a bottom. The bandana’s color spelled out the pleasures sought. Stellar is fluent in the language.

“We were all walking personal ads,” Holleran writes. “We were like actors going on stage even when all we wanted was a quart of milk.” In Andy Marshall Red (1977), the model nails his entrance: leaning against pitted brick, lips parted, he lets the zipper of his jacket gape open to below the navel, baring a smooth, sculpted chest.

The grandest of these theaters lines the Hudson. For years, the derelict piers of the Lower West Side served as solarium, cruising ground and alcove, where strangers made love in stolen moments, in the shade of the sheds or in broad daylight. Holleran recalls their soaring ceilings, the lap of water against the pilings and a “majestic vacancy” that led more than one gay writer to compare them to cathedrals.

Beneath these naves, two young men framed by the dark jamb of a doorway embrace on the upper floor of a pier shed, against a peeling partition ( Pier Upstairs , 1979), an orange bandana poking out of the left back pocket of a pair of jeans. The “hotties in this volume,” the novelist writes, once posed among the ruins, “perched like goats on rotten timbers, presiding over the rites of Priapus.”

Stellar shows these rites unflinchingly. In Pier Sex (1978), two naked men entwined on a towel, right on the asphalt, have kept on nothing but their striped socks and work boots. Jordan Hancock, who initiated and edited the book, belongs to “the Tumblr generation,” which came to know the photographer online. As he sees it, “fucking is everywhere now,” and seeing it on a dilapidated pier is “just beautiful, not transgressive.”

Stellar works within breathing distance, and many of his models stare straight into the lens. Alvin Baltrop, a fellow photographer and pier regular, captured bodies and ruins there from 1975 to 1986, sometimes suspended from a harness. In 1981, Stellar photographed Peter Hujar, the master of New York portraiture who also roamed the piers, his T-shirt hiked up to bare his chest against a graffitied wall. AIDS would claim him six years later.

In June 1981, the first cases of the epidemic were reported, and desire now brushed against death. Stellar moved part of the scene into the privacy of his apartment, where he posed single men and couples against a bare wall. There, the often-square format and a raking light that sculpts the shoulders lend the embraces a hushed gravity.

Before this backdrop came, in Hancock’s words, “the artists, the friends, the porn stars, the lovers.” In Nashom holds Howard, NYC (1994), two hands clasp the brow of a young man, his eyes turned heavenward like a Saint Sebastian. These portraits sway between exhibition and introspection. In Jason, NYC (1990), the model offers himself naked and erect, one arm casually slung over the back of a leather armchair.

The painter Hugh Steers, who depicted male intimacy in the age of the epidemic, poses for Stellar in 1993, folded in on himself, head bowed, ankles crossed above scuffed shoes. He would die of AIDS two years later, at 32. Of the hundreds of men who sat for him in those years, only a handful are still here. Yet in this book, Holleran writes, they “look out at you as if alive.”

Former models called Stellar after their diagnosis: “I am afraid I won’t look like this for long. Can I come back in?” Decades later, Hancock lingered over the picture of a beautiful young man glancing askance, eyes half rolled back. The photographer’s verdict was swift: “You can’t use that one.” Then he explained: “Because these are my friends. They were beautiful, but they are gone. I only want them to look their best.”

Don’t Worry Boys by Stanley Stellar is published by Loose Joints (2026).

Krishnamurti）追随者提出的问题。该片由马修·多尔蒂（Matthew Dougherty）执导，由朱莉·萨耶尔（Julie Thayer）拍摄的数百小时录像剪辑而成。朱莉是一位富有的纽约人，她在1989年颠覆了自己的生活，开始追随克里希那穆提。当前的、反思性的采访与这些档案影像交织在一起，勾勒出了这位“开悟”之人的一生——他毕生都在质疑开悟。在1967年经历了一次抽象的、改变人生的事件后，乌·G·克里希那穆提抛弃了家庭以及原本将他培养为圣人的生活。在追随另一位年长的印度灵性人物吉杜·克里希那穆提（Jiddu Krishnamurti）多年后，乌·G·开始确信吉杜的教导是虚假的，并将挑战这些教导作为他一生的事业。乌·G·的追随者们寻找他并遭到他的“痛斥”——本质上，就是因他们的物质欲望和自负担忧而受到侮辱和嘲笑。萨耶尔成了他最虔诚的学生之一，也是最容易成为他嘲笑靶子的人。“你为什么要这样对我，朱莉？”他在某个时刻问她。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《自然状态》是一部具有挑战性的文本，这很大程度上是因为乌·G·本人就充满挑战。他拒绝捐赠和追随者，却又招致了追随带来的名气（后一点在影片后半部分的访谈嘉宾中引发了争论）。正如萨耶尔的录像所证明的那样，他对那些倾听他的人作出的所有承诺就是“虚无”。他声称自己生活在一种自然状态中，在这种状态下，他对寻找意义的无用性有着高度的觉察。尽管如此，许多听过他的话并花时间与他相处的人，依然会谈到他身上携带的那股能量。影片的执行制片人之一、电影人简·坎皮恩（Jane Campion）对此有着第一手的回忆。作为乌·G·的朋友，她谈到了她在他身上感受到的“能量场”，以及这让她感觉几乎像喝醉了一样。甚至在他去世后，他的一些追随者还回忆起发生过的奇异现象。其他人则忽视了这些记忆，坚信他的正如他坚持的那样，他的一生是平凡的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "萨耶尔的便携式摄像机素材的美学也有其独到之处。它颗粒感重且生硬，带有一种强烈的律动感，不知何故，这让乌·G·看起来既刻薄又更加真实。这契合了多尔蒂试图呈现的复杂基调。有一次，有人问朱莉为什么要拍摄这一切。她回答说，她在镜头后面“感觉更安全”。显而易见的是，这些试图通过乌·G·的侮辱来摆脱自我的人，所追求的远不止于此。在观看这部电影时，我不禁想起一句归属于格鲁克·马克思（Groucho Marx）的名言：“我才不想加入一个肯接纳我当会员的俱乐部。”这里还存在着一种关于将自己定义为无神论者的矛盾观念。通过笃信一种整齐划一的不信，你就否定了不相信某事这一整个假定的理由。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "纵观整部纪录片，乌·G·克里希那穆提的不信似乎大体上是真诚的，而他的追随者在追求谦逊的过程中则显得由衷地好奇且深思熟虑。多尔蒂坦率而勇敢地推出了一部没有给出美好答案的电影。是否有人因为乌·G·的教导而变得更好？或者说由于缺乏教导而变好？因为他的刻薄而变得更好？也许吧，也许没有。归根结底，唯一重要的是被帮助的人是否相信自己得到了帮助。但随后我们又回到了最初的问题：去相信某事。然后我们便周而复始地陷入其中。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《自然状态》在2026年伍德斯托克电影节上展映。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
“Could I have wasted 35 years of my life?” It’s a question asked by someone who was a follower of “anti-guru” U. G. Krishnamurti in the documentary The Natural State . Directed by Matthew Dougherty, the film is constructed from hundreds of hours of video captured by Julie Thayer, a wealthy New Yorker who upended her life in 1989 to follow Krishnamurti. Current, reflective interviews are cut with this archival footage to build a portrait of this “enlightened” man who spent his life questioning enlightenment. Following an abstract, life-changing incident in 1967, U. G. Krishnamurti abandoned his family and a life that had been spent preparing him to be a holy man. After years following Jiddu Krishnamurti, another older Indian spiritual figure, U. G. had become convinced Jiddu’s teachings were fraudulent and made it his life’s work to challenge them. U. G.’s followers seek him out and get “blasted” by him. Essentially, to be insulted and ridiculed for their material desires and egotistical worries. Thayer became one of his most devout pupils, and one of his easiest targets for ridicule. “Why are you doing this to me, Julie?” he asks her at one point.

The Natural State is a challenging text, in no small part because U. G. himself is challenging. He refused donations and followers, yet invited the fame that came with his following (this last fact is debated by the talking heads in the back half of the film). As evidenced in Thayer’s videos, all he promised those who listened to him was nothing. He claimed to live in a natural state, in which he was hyper aware of the uselessness in searching for meaning. Despite this, many of those who listened to his words and spend time around him speak to the energy he carried around with. One of the film’s executive producers, filmmaker Jane Campion, recalls this first-hand. A friend of U.G.’s, she speaks about the “energy field” that she felt around him, and how it made her feel almost drunk. Even in his death, some of his followers recall strange phenomena that occurred. Others disregard these memories, determined that his death was ordinary, like he insisted his life was.

There is also something to the aesthetic of Thayer’s camcorder footage. Grainy and abrupt, it has a percussive quality that somehow make U.G. appear more mean and more honest at the same time. It fits with the complex tones that Dougherty is trying to bring to the fore. At one point, somebody asks Julie why she’s filming everything. She responds that she “feels safer” behind the camera. It’s clear these people searching to be freed of their ego via U.G.’s insults are searching for something more than that. Watching the film, I kept thinking of the quote attributed to Groucho Marx: “I wouldn’t want to belong to a club that would have me as a member.” There’s also the contradictory idea of identifying as an atheist. By subscribing to a uniform non-belief, you negate the whole presumed reason of not believing in something.

Throughout the documentary, U. G. Krishnamurti mostly seems genuine in his non-beliefs, while his followers seem earnestly curious and thoughtful in their pursuit of modesty. And Dougherty is frankly brave to offer up a film with no good answers. Is anybody bettered by U. G’s teachings? Or lack thereof? Bettered by his meanness? Maybe, maybe not. Ultimately, it only matters if the person being helped believes they are being helped. But then we’re right back to that initial problem: believing in something. And ’round and ’round we go.

The Natural State screens at the 2026 Woodstock Film Festival.
